title: Getty Images to File Chapter 11, Go Private With Koch
htmlContent:
Less than four months after walking away from a $3.7 billion merger with rival Shutterstock, Getty Images is heading into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and will emerge as a private company. The company announced Monday that it has reached a deal with all of its major financial stakeholders on a prepackaged plan to restructure roughly $2.1 billion in debt.

Members of the Getty family, through affiliated entities, and affiliates of Charles Koch's Koch Equity Development have committed up to $533 million in new equity. Once the restructuring is complete, expected by the end of 2026, those investors will own 100% of the reorganized company.

A Prepackaged Path Through Bankruptcy

Getty plans to solicit creditor votes on its reorganization plan in the coming days and file for Chapter 11 within weeks. The requisite majority of creditors has already committed to support it. The filing will cover only certain U.S. entities, and Koch Equity Development will provide up to $143 million in financing, alongside cash from ongoing operations.

Vendors are slated to be paid in full in the ordinary course, and Getty anticipates no impact on contributors, partners, customers or employees. A company spokesperson also told The Hollywood Reporter that layoffs are not part of the plan.

Reworking the Balance Sheet

Holders of 83.5% of its unsecured bonds agreed to retire $270 million in senior unsecured notes. Holders of roughly 89% of its secured bonds and term loans agreed to lower interest costs and extend maturities, and every lender in its revolving credit facility signed on. The relief comes as Getty ended the second quarter with just $51.6 million in cash, squeezed by debt service, merger costs, warrant litigation and its legal fight with Stability AI.

The Shutterstock Deal That Fell Apart

The road to bankruptcy began in late June, when Getty's board scrapped the Shutterstock combination after the U.K.'s Competition and Markets Authority required the sale of Shutterstock's editorial business. With Getty betting its future on editorial, CEO Craig Peters viewed that remedy as a non-starter.

The failed pursuit was costly. On the company's August earnings call, Peters said Getty had spent "more than $100 million across professional fees and financing costs in pursuit of what we believe will be a strategic transaction." Getty then hired Guggenheim Securities to explore financing for a standalone future, a search that led back to Koch, which has backed Getty since making a $500 million preferred equity investment in 2018.

Doubling Down on Editorial

In a new investor presentation, Getty acknowledged that its iStock eCommerce arm has faced "declining agency demand and disruption," a shift likely tied to AI tools that make generic stock imagery easy to produce.

Its editorial division, built on real photographs of news events, red carpets and film premieres, is projected to grow from $369 million to $400 million by 2029.

CFO Jennifer Leyden said in August that annual subscribers fell from 321,000 to 241,000 over the prior year because of a "deliberate strategy to deemphasize lower-value acquisition channels, including the discontinuation of our iStock free trial program."

What Leadership Is Saying

"This transformational transaction is underpinned by the strength of the business and the significant growth potential we see ahead," he said. "I am pleased to continue our strong partnership with Koch Equity Development and the lender groups to provide capital structure improvements that will enable us to build on our solid foundation and seize new growth opportunities." — Co-founder and chairman Mark Getty< "Core pillars of our success are the longstanding commitment of our customers and partners, the deep expertise and creativity of our team and content contributors, and the uniqueness of our archive." — CEO Craig Peters "We remain confident in the company's future and fully support this transaction alongside the Getty family. This equity investment will provide Getty Images with a firm financial foundation and greater flexibility to continue investing in its employees, customers, contributors, and future growth." — Mike Harris, senior managing director and co-head of Koch Equity Development

What Comes Next

For photographers and other contributors, the proposal indicates ordinary unsecured claims should be unimpaired. Until a court approves the plan, though, contributors would be wise to keep royalty statements, payment records and official bankruptcy notices. If everything stays on schedule, Getty will close out 2026 as a private company with a lighter debt load and a sharper focus on news and archive photography.
